goals: Explain conduction in metals using free electrons, relaxation time and drift velocity
Derive I = neAvd and define mobility
Derive J = σE and the expression ρ = m/(ne²τ)

slides.narration: Flip a switch and the lamp lights at once, yet the electrons in the wire crawl along at less than a millimetre per second. In this part we build a simple picture of a metal as a gas of free electrons bumping into vibrating ions, and from it we derive the current, Ohm’s law and the resistivity of the metal.

slides.heading: Electric current
slides.body_md: Current is the rate of flow of charge: $I = \dfrac{\Delta q}{\Delta t}$, unit ampere (1 A = 1 C s⁻¹). Conventional current flows in the direction positive charge would move; in metals the carriers are **electrons**, moving the other way.
bullets: Current is a scalar (it obeys algebraic, not vector, addition at junctions) although it has a sense along a wire.
A steady current needs a source of emf to keep a field in the conductor.

slides.narration: An electric current is the rate at which charge flows past a point, coulombs per second, or amperes. By convention we take its direction as the way positive charge would move. In a metal wire it is actually electrons that move, drifting the opposite way. A cell keeps a field inside the wire, and that field keeps the electrons drifting.

slides.heading: Free electrons and relaxation time
slides.body_md: A metal holds a “gas” of **free electrons** moving randomly at about $10^5$ m s⁻¹, colliding with the vibrating ions. With no field their average velocity is zero.
bullets: The average time between successive collisions is the **relaxation time** τ (about $10^{-14}$ s in copper).
In a field E, each electron accelerates at $a = eE/m$ (opposite to E) between collisions, then loses that extra velocity in the next collision.

slides.narration: Inside a metal, the outer electrons are not tied to any atom. They dash about at hundreds of kilometres per second, colliding with the ions, but in every direction equally, so on average they go nowhere. Switch on a field and between collisions each electron is pushed a little in the opposite direction. The average time between collisions is called the relaxation time.

slides.heading: Drift velocity and mobility
slides.body_md:
The extra velocity averaged over many collisions is the **drift velocity**:
$$\vec v_d = -\dfrac{e\vec E}{m}\tau,\qquad |v_d| = \dfrac{eE\tau}{m}$$
**Mobility** $\mu = \dfrac{v_d}{E} = \dfrac{e\tau}{m}$ (m² V⁻¹ s⁻¹): drift speed per unit field.
bullets: Drift velocity is tiny (mm s⁻¹) compared with the random speed (10⁵ m s⁻¹).
A lamp lights at once because the **field** spreads along the wire at nearly the speed of light, setting all the electrons drifting together.

slides.narration: Averaging over collisions, electrons acquire a small steady velocity opposite to the field, e E tau over m. That is the drift velocity, only a fraction of a millimetre per second in a typical wire. Mobility measures how easily the carriers drift: drift speed per volt per metre. The lamp still lights instantly because the field sets every electron in the circuit moving at the same moment.

slides.heading: Current and drift velocity: I = neAvd
slides.body_md:
In time $\Delta t$, all free electrons within a length $v_d\Delta t$ cross a section of area $A$: their number is $nAv_d\Delta t$ (n = number per unit volume). Charge crossing $= n e A v_d\Delta t$, so
$$I = n e A v_d,\qquad J = \dfrac{I}{A} = n e v_d$$

slides.heading: Ohm’s law from drift: J = σE
slides.body_md:
Substituting $v_d = \dfrac{eE\tau}{m}$ in $J = n e v_d$:
$$J = \dfrac{n e^2\tau}{m}E = \sigma E,\qquad \sigma = \dfrac{n e^2\tau}{m},\quad \rho = \dfrac{1}{\sigma} = \dfrac{m}{n e^2\tau}$$
bullets: For a wire: $E = V/l$ and $J = I/A$ give $V = \dfrac{\rho l}{A}I = RI$: **Ohm’s law**.
ρ depends on n and τ, properties of the material and its temperature, not on the wire’s shape.

visual.alt: Table of current density, conductivity, resistivity, mobility and conductance with their relations and SI units

slides.narration: Put the drift velocity into J equals n e v d and the current density comes out proportional to the field: J equals sigma E, where the conductivity sigma is n e squared tau over m. This is Ohm’s law in its microscopic form. For a wire of length l and area A, it becomes V equals I times rho l over A, the familiar V equals I R.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: relaxation time and mobility in gold
slides.body_md: Gold, used to plate connector pins, has resistivity $2.4 \times 10^{-8}$ Ω m and $5.9 \times 10^{28}$ free electrons per m³. Find the relaxation time and the mobility of its free electrons.
bullets: Step 1 — $\tau = \dfrac{m}{\rho n e^2} = \dfrac{9.1 \times 10^{-31}}{2.4 \times 10^{-8} \times 5.9 \times 10^{28} \times (1.6 \times 10^{-19})^2} \approx 2.51 \times 10^{-14}$ s.
Step 2 — $\mu = \dfrac{e\tau}{m} = \dfrac{1.6 \times 10^{-19} \times 2.51 \times 10^{-14}}{9.1 \times 10^{-31}} \approx 4.41 \times 10^{-3}$ m² V$^{-1}$ s$^{-1}$.

visual.alt: Table of current density, conductivity, resistivity, mobility and conductance with their relations and SI units

slides.narration: Rearranging the resistivity formula, the relaxation time is m over rho n e squared: about two and a half times ten to the minus fourteen second between collisions. The mobility, e tau over m, is about four and a half times ten to the minus three square metres per volt second, so a field of one volt per metre would make the electrons drift at roughly four and a half millimetres per second.

slides.narration: To sum up: free electrons in a metal move randomly and collide every relaxation time tau. slides.narration: Why is a heater element thin and long? Why does a light bulb draw a big surge of current when first switched on? And how does the electricity board work out your bill? In this part we connect resistance to the shape and temperature of a conductor, and work out power and energy in everyday units.

slides.heading: Resistance and resistivity
slides.body_md:
For a uniform wire:
$$R = \dfrac{\rho l}{A}$$
ρ is the **resistivity** (Ω m), a property of the material. **Conductance** $G = 1/R$ (siemens); **conductivity** $\sigma = 1/\rho$ (S m⁻¹).
bullets: Doubling the length doubles R; doubling the area halves R.
Stretching a wire to n times its length (same volume) multiplies R by n².

slides.narration: A long thin wire has more resistance than a short thick one: resistance is resistivity times length over area. Resistivity belongs to the material: about two times ten to the minus eight ohm metres for copper, about sixty times more for nichrome. If you stretch a wire to twice its length, its area halves at the same time, so its resistance goes up four times.

Step 2 — $R = \dfrac{\rho l}{A} = \dfrac{1.1 \times 10^{-6} \times 1.5}{7.07 \times 10^{-8}} \approx 23.3$ Ω.

slides.heading: Ohmic and non-ohmic conductors
slides.body_md: A conductor obeys **Ohm’s law** if V ∝ I at constant temperature: its V–I graph is a **straight line through the origin**.
bullets: Ohmic: metal wires at constant temperature.
Non-ohmic: filament lamps (R rises with heating), diodes (one-way, non-linear), thermistors, electrolytes; graphs curved, not through the origin, or different in reverse.

slides.narration: Plot current against voltage. For a metal wire kept at a steady temperature you get a straight line through the origin: the resistance is constant, and the wire obeys Ohm’s law. A lamp filament heats up as the current rises, so its resistance increases and the graph bends over. Diodes conduct one way only. These are non-ohmic devices.

slides.heading: Temperature dependence
slides.body_md: For metals, approximately $\rho_T = \rho_0[1 + \alpha(T - T_0)]$ (and $R_T = R_0[1 + \alpha(T - T_0)]$), with α > 0, the **temperature coefficient of resistivity**.
bullets: **Metals:** n is fixed; heating makes ions vibrate more, so **τ falls** and ρ rises.
**Semiconductors:** heating frees many more carriers, so **n rises** steeply and ρ falls (negative α).
Alloys such as manganin and constantan have very small α: used for standard resistors.

visual.alt: Resistivity against temperature rise: a metal such as copper rises nearly in a straight line, while a semiconductor falls steeply
visual.caption: Metals: τ falls as ions vibrate more. Semiconductors: n rises enormously, outweighing the fall in τ.

slides.narration: Heat a metal and its resistance rises roughly in a straight line, because the ions vibrate more and electrons collide more often, so the relaxation time falls. Heat a semiconductor and the opposite happens: far more electrons are freed to carry current, and the resistivity drops steeply. Some alloys hardly change at all, which makes them ideal for standard resistors.

slides.heading: Worked example 4: a motor winding warms up
slides.body_md: The copper winding of a pump motor measures 50 Ω in a workshop at 20 °C ($\alpha = 3.9 \times 10^{-3}$ °C$^{-1}$). What will it measure when the motor runs at 80 °C, and at what temperature will it read 60 Ω?
bullets: Step 2 — $60 = 50[1 + 3.9 \times 10^{-3}(T - 20)] \Rightarrow T - 20 = \dfrac{0.20}{3.9 \times 10^{-3}} \approx 51.3$, so $T \approx 71.3$ °C.

visual.alt: Resistivity against temperature rise: a metal such as copper rises nearly in a straight line, while a semiconductor falls steeply
visual.caption: Metals: τ falls as ions vibrate more. Semiconductors: n rises enormously, outweighing the fall in τ.

slides.narration: Warming by sixty degrees raises the resistance by alpha times sixty, about twenty three per cent, to nearly sixty two ohms. Working backwards, a rise of ten ohms, a fifth of the original, needs about fifty one degrees of warming, so the coil reaches sixty ohms at about seventy one degrees Celsius. Resistance thermometers use exactly this effect.

slides.heading: Electrical power and energy
slides.body_md:
The rate at which electrical energy is converted:
$$P = VI = I^2R = \dfrac{V^2}{R}$$
Energy $W = Pt$. Commercial unit: **1 kilowatt hour** (kW h, “unit”) $= 1000 \times 3600 = 3.6 \times 10^{6}$ J.
bullets: Joule heating $I^2Rt$ heats heaters, irons and toasters; it wastes energy in cables.
Power is transmitted at high voltage so that the current, and the $I^2R$ loss, is small.

visual.alt: Table of the three power formulas and when to use each

slides.narration: Electrical power is voltage times current, which can also be written I squared R or V squared over R. Choose the form that uses the quantity that is the same: I squared R for things in series, V squared over R for appliances on the mains. Energy is power times time. The board measures it in kilowatt hours, each worth three point six million joules.

slides.heading: Worked example 5: a heater on a low supply
slides.body_md: A heater is rated 1000 W at 230 V. Find its resistance and current, and its power if the supply falls to 200 V (assume R unchanged).
bullets: Step 2 — $P' = \dfrac{200^2}{52.9} \approx 756$ W.

sections.heading: 1. Free electrons, drift and mobility
sections.body_md:
- Current $I = \Delta q/\Delta t$ (A = C s⁻¹); conventional current is opposite to electron flow.
- Free electrons move randomly (~10⁵ m s⁻¹) colliding with ions; **relaxation time** τ = mean time between collisions (~10⁻¹⁴ s).
- In a field: acceleration $eE/m$; **drift velocity** $v_d = eE\tau/m$ (opposite to E), ~10⁻⁴ m s⁻¹. **Mobility** $\mu = v_d/E = e\tau/m$ (m² V⁻¹ s⁻¹).
- **$I = n e A v_d$** (n = free electrons per m³): all electrons within $v_d\Delta t$ of a section cross it in $\Delta t$.
- Lamps light instantly because the **field** is set up along the wire at nearly the speed of light.

key_terms.definition_md: Average time between successive collisions of a free electron with the ions.
Average velocity acquired by free electrons in a conductor in an electric field.
Drift velocity per unit electric field, eτ/m.

sections.body_md:

- For a wire, $E = V/l$, $J = I/A$ give $V = IR$ with $R = \rho l/A$: **Ohm’s law** (V ∝ I at constant temperature).

sections.heading: 4. Temperature dependence
sections.body_md:
- Metals: $\rho_T = \rho_0[1 + \alpha(T - T_0)]$, α > 0 (copper about 3.9 × 10⁻³ °C⁻¹): n constant, τ decreases as ions vibrate more.
- Semiconductors: ρ **decreases** with temperature (negative α): n increases sharply, outweighing the fall in τ.
- Alloys (manganin, constantan): very small α, high ρ — standard resistors; nichrome for heaters.

key_terms.definition_md: Fractional change in resistivity per degree rise in temperature.

visual.alt: Resistivity against temperature rise: a metal such as copper rises nearly in a straight line, while a semiconductor falls steeply
visual.caption: Metals: τ falls as ions vibrate more. Semiconductors: n rises enormously, outweighing the fall in τ.

sections.heading: 5. Electrical energy and power
sections.body_md:
- $P = VI = I^2R = V^2/R$; energy $W = Pt = VIt$; Joule heating $H = I^2Rt$.
- Commercial unit: 1 kW h (one “unit”) = $3.6 \times 10^{6}$ J. Bill = total kW h × rate.
- Rated appliance: $R = V_\text{rated}^2/P_\text{rated}$; on a different supply $P' = V'^2/R$.
- Long-distance transmission at high voltage reduces current and so the $I^2R$ loss.

options.text_md: twice as large
half as large
the same
four times as large

questions.solution_md: I = neAv_d with I and n the same: v_d ∝ 1/A, so halving A doubles v_d — option (a).

questions.stem_md: The battery lead of a scooter has a metal core 2.5 mm² in cross-section and carries 2.0 A. The metal has 8.0 × 10²⁸ conduction electrons in every cubic metre. What is their drift speed? Answer in units of 10⁻⁵ m s⁻¹ (3 significant figures).

marking_scheme.step: v_d = I/(neA) with A in m²

questions.stem_md: In a metal wire carrying a current from end A to end B (conventional current), the free electrons move

options.text_md: from A towards B
randomly with no net motion
from B towards A
from A to B at the speed of light

questions.solution_md: Conventional current is the direction of positive-charge flow; electrons drift the opposite way — option (c).

questions.stem_md: A steady current of 3.0 A flows for 2.0 minutes. How many electrons pass a cross-section of the wire? Give the answer in units of 10²¹.
In a metal the relaxation time of the free electrons is 2.5 × 10⁻¹⁴ s. Find their drift velocity in a field of 0.50 V m⁻¹, in mm s⁻¹ (3 significant figures).
Electrons in a wire drift at 4.0 × 10⁻⁴ m s⁻¹ when the field in the wire is 0.10 V m⁻¹. Find their mobility, in units of 10⁻³ m² V⁻¹ s⁻¹.
A ceiling fan starts turning the moment its wall switch is pressed, although 4 m of cable separate the two and the conduction electrons in the cable drift at roughly 0.1 mm s⁻¹. How is this possible?

answer.model_answer_md: The cable and motor winding are **already full of free electrons**. Closing the switch sets up an **electric field** throughout the circuit almost instantly (it spreads at close to the **speed of light**). Electrons **everywhere**, including those in the winding, start drifting **at once**; none has to travel the 4 m.

questions.solution_md: The field spreads almost instantly; the electrons already present in the winding start drifting together.

marking_scheme.step: Field established along the circuit at nearly c

questions.stem_md: A conductor of uniform cross-section A holds n free electrons per unit volume, each drifting with speed $v_d$. By counting the electrons that cross one section in a time Δt, show that the current is $I = n e A v_d$.

answer.model_answer_md: Consider a conductor of cross-section $A$ with $n$ free electrons per unit volume drifting with speed $v_d$. In time $\Delta t$ each electron moves $v_d\Delta t$, so all electrons within a length $v_d\Delta t$ of a cross-section pass through it. Their number is $n \times A v_d\Delta t$, carrying charge $\Delta q = n e A v_d\Delta t$. Hence $I = \dfrac{\Delta q}{\Delta t} = n e A v_d$.

questions.solution_md: Count electrons in a slice v_dΔt long.

marking_scheme.step: Electrons within v_dΔt cross in Δt

options.text_md: about the same
smaller by a factor of about 10⁹
larger by a factor of about 10⁹
smaller by a factor of about 10

questions.solution_md: Random speeds are about 10⁵ m s⁻¹; drift speeds about 10⁻⁴ m s⁻¹ — option (b).

questions.stem_md: The average time between two successive collisions of a free electron with the ions of a metal is called the ___ time.
questions.solution_md: The **relaxation** time τ.

questions.stem_md: A copper wire is replaced by one of the same material with twice the radius, and the current is kept the same. The drift velocity becomes

options.text_md: one half of its earlier value
one quarter of its earlier value
twice its earlier value
unchanged

questions.solution_md: A ∝ r², so doubling r makes A four times larger; v_d = I/(neA) falls to ¼ — option (b).

questions.stem_md: Two copper wires of diameters 1.0 mm and 2.0 mm are joined end to end and carry a current. Find the ratio of the drift velocity in the thinner wire to that in the thicker wire.
questions.solution_md: Same current and the same n: $v_d \propto \dfrac{1}{A} \propto \dfrac{1}{d^2}$, so $\dfrac{v_1}{v_2} = \left(\dfrac{2.0}{1.0}\right)^2 = 4.0$.

questions.stem_md: True or false? Keeping the same 6 V battery, a student swaps a 1 m nichrome wire for a 2 m nichrome wire of equal thickness. The electrons in the longer wire drift twice as fast.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: False. The field in the wire is E = V/l, which halves when l doubles, so v_d = eEτ/m halves: the electrons drift half as fast.

questions.stem_md: A data sheet lists the electron mobility in a sample of germanium. Mobility being drift speed per unit field strength, the sheet must quote it in

options.text_md: m s⁻¹
V m⁻¹ s⁻¹
m² V⁻¹ s⁻¹
m V s⁻¹

questions.solution_md: μ = v_d/E: (m s⁻¹)/(V m⁻¹) = m² V⁻¹ s⁻¹ — option (c).

**Assertion (A):** In a wire carrying a few amperes, a free electron takes hours to drift one metre along the wire.

**Reason (R):** Between collisions, the free electrons of a metal move at speeds well below 1 m s⁻¹.

Choose the correct option.

Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation for Assertion.
Assertion is true and Reason is false.
Assertion is false and Reason is true.

questions.solution_md: A is true: drift speeds are of order 10⁻⁴ m s⁻¹, so 1 m takes about 10⁴ s. R is false: between collisions the electrons move very fast (about 10⁵ m s⁻¹) but in random directions; only the small extra drift is directed — option (c).

questions.stem_md: A copper cable of cross-section 4.0 mm² carries 5.0 A; copper has 8.5 × 10²⁸ free electrons per m³. Find (a) the current density, (b) the drift velocity, (c) the time an electron takes to drift 1.0 m.
questions.solution_md: J = I/A; v_d = J/ne; t = l/v_d.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Of two metals with the same number density of free electrons, the one with the longer relaxation time has the lower resistivity.

**Reason (R):** The resistivity of a metal is ρ = m/(ne²τ).

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation for Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation for Assertion.
Assertion is true and Reason is false.
Assertion is false and Reason is true.

questions.solution_md: Both true, and R explains A: with n fixed, ρ ∝ 1/τ — option (a).

questions.stem_md: A current of 5.0 A flows through a wire of cross-section 2.0 mm². Find the current density, in units of 10⁶ A m⁻².
Copper has a conductivity of 5.8 × 10⁷ S m⁻¹. Find the current density in a copper wire in which the electric field is 0.020 V m⁻¹, in units of 10⁶ A m⁻² (3 significant figures).
Starting from the drift of free electrons, derive the expression ρ = m/(ne²τ) for the resistivity of a metal.

answer.model_answer_md: In a field E, between collisions each electron accelerates at $a = eE/m$; averaged over collisions it gains a drift velocity $v_d = \dfrac{eE\tau}{m}$. The current density is $J = n e v_d = \dfrac{n e^2\tau}{m}E$. Comparing with Ohm’s law $J = \sigma E$: $\sigma = \dfrac{n e^2\tau}{m}$, so $\rho = \dfrac{1}{\sigma} = \dfrac{m}{n e^2\tau}$.

questions.solution_md: v_d, J = nev_d, compare with J = σE.

questions.stem_md: Aluminium has a resistivity of 2.8 × 10⁻⁸ Ω m and 1.8 × 10²⁹ free electrons per m³. Find the relaxation time of its electrons, in units of 10⁻¹⁵ s (3 significant figures).
In a metallic conductor obeying Ohm’s law, the current density vector J is

options.text_md: opposite to the electric field E
in the same direction as the electric field E
perpendicular to the electric field E
in the direction of the electrons’ drift

questions.solution_md: J = σE with σ > 0: J is along E, opposite to the electron drift — option (b).

questions.stem_md: State Ohm’s law and the condition under which it holds. Write it in terms of current density.

answer.model_answer_md: The current through a conductor is **directly proportional** to the potential difference across it, **provided its temperature and other physical conditions remain constant**: $V = IR$. In microscopic form, $\vec J = \sigma\vec E$.

questions.solution_md: V ∝ I at constant temperature; J = σE.

questions.stem_md: Show that the microscopic form J = σE leads to V = IR for a uniform wire of length l and cross-section A, and identify R.

answer.model_answer_md: In a uniform wire $J = \dfrac{I}{A}$ and $E = \dfrac{V}{l}$. So $\dfrac{I}{A} = \sigma\dfrac{V}{l}$, i.e. $V = \dfrac{l}{\sigma A}I = \dfrac{\rho l}{A}I$. This is $V = IR$ with $R = \dfrac{\rho l}{A}$.

questions.solution_md: Substitute J = I/A, E = V/l.

questions.stem_md: Electrical conductivity is measured in siemens per ___.
questions.solution_md: Siemens per **metre** (S m⁻¹ = Ω⁻¹ m⁻¹).

questions.stem_md: Metal X has twice as many free electrons per unit volume as metal Y, and the same relaxation time. The resistivity of X is

options.text_md: twice that of Y
equal to that of Y

half that of Y

questions.stem_md: Electric current has both magnitude and a direction along a wire. Why is it nevertheless treated as a scalar quantity?

answer.model_answer_md: Currents meeting at a junction **add algebraically**, not by the **parallelogram law**: the current leaving equals the sum of those arriving whatever the angles between the wires. A vector would have to add according to directions; current does not, so it is a **scalar** (its “direction” is only a sense along the conductor).

questions.solution_md: Algebraic addition at junctions.

half that of P
the same as that of P

questions.stem_md: A torch bulb draws 0.20 A at 1.0 V but only 0.30 A at 3.0 V. Use these readings to show that the bulb is non-ohmic, and explain the cause.

answer.model_answer_md: $R = V/I$: at 1.0 V, $R = 5.0$ Ω; at 3.0 V, $R = 10$ Ω. The resistance **doubles**, so I is **not proportional** to V: the bulb is **non-ohmic**. The larger current **heats the filament**; in hotter metal the ions vibrate more, the **relaxation time falls** and the resistivity rises.

questions.solution_md: Compare V/I at the two readings; the filament heats up.

Filament heats; τ falls, resistivity rises

the resistivity

the power

options.text_md: True

questions.stem_md: Find the conductance of a 25 Ω resistor, in siemens.
Two wires are made from equal masses of the same metal; the second is twice as long as the first. Find the ratio of the resistance of the second wire to that of the first.
questions.solution_md: Same mass and material means the same volume $Al$. With $l_2 = 2l_1$, $A_2 = A_1/2$. $\dfrac{R_2}{R_1} = \dfrac{l_2/A_2}{l_1/A_1} = 2 \times 2 = 4$.

questions.stem_md: Wires A and B are made of the same alloy. A is 1.0 m long with diameter 0.50 mm; B is 2.0 m long with diameter 1.0 mm. Find the ratio of their resistances and state which gets hotter when they carry the same current.

answer.model_answer_md: $R = \dfrac{\rho l}{\pi d^2/4} \propto \dfrac{l}{d^2}$. $\dfrac{R_A}{R_B} = \dfrac{1.0/(0.50)^2}{2.0/(1.0)^2} = \dfrac{4.0}{2.0} = 2.0$. With the same current, power $I^2R$ is larger in **A** (twice that in B), so A produces more heat.

questions.solution_md: R ∝ l/d²; I²R.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** A pure silicon chip conducts better on a hot afternoon than on a cold night.

**Reason (R):** Warming a semiconductor frees many more charge carriers, an effect that outweighs the shorter relaxation time.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation for Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation for Assertion.
Assertion is true and Reason is false.
Assertion is false and Reason is true.

questions.solution_md: Both true, and R explains A: in ρ = m/(ne²τ) the rise in n far outweighs the fall in τ, so the resistivity of the chip is lower when it is warm — option (a).

questions.stem_md: A coil has resistance 40 Ω at 20 °C and 48 Ω at 120 °C. Find the temperature coefficient of resistance of its material (taking 20 °C as reference), in units of 10⁻³ °C⁻¹.
A copper wire has temperature coefficient of resistance 4.0 × 10⁻³ °C⁻¹ referred to 0 °C. At what temperature, in °C, is its resistance double its value at 0 °C (assuming the linear relation holds)?
questions.solution_md: $2R_0 = R_0(1 + \alpha T) \Rightarrow \alpha T = 1 \Rightarrow T = \dfrac{1}{4.0 \times 10^{-3}} = 250$ °C.

questions.stem_md: When a metal wire is heated, its resistivity increases mainly because

options.text_md: the number of free electrons decreases
the wire expands and becomes longer
the free electrons gain mass
the ions vibrate more, so the relaxation time decreases

questions.solution_md: In ρ = m/(ne²τ), n hardly changes in a metal; τ falls as collisions become more frequent — option (d).

questions.stem_md: The coils inside a laboratory resistance box are wound from constantan rather than copper, chiefly because constantan

options.text_md: changes its resistance very little when its temperature changes
conducts better than copper
has a resistance that falls as it warms
cannot melt at any working current

questions.solution_md: Constantan’s temperature coefficient of resistance is tiny, so the marked values stay reliable as the coils warm — option (a).

questions.stem_md: A copper strip and a silicon chip are both warmed from 20 °C to 80 °C. Referring to the carrier density n and the relaxation time τ in ρ = m/(ne²τ), state and explain what happens to the resistivity of each, and describe the shape of each ρ–T graph.

answer.model_answer_md: **Copper strip:** n is practically **constant**; on warming the ions vibrate with larger amplitude, so collisions are more frequent and **τ falls**: ρ **increases**, almost linearly (a gently rising, nearly straight graph). **Silicon chip:** warming frees many more charge carriers, so **n rises very sharply**; this outweighs the fall in τ, so ρ **decreases** steeply (a falling, roughly exponential graph).

questions.solution_md: τ for metals, n for semiconductors.

marking_scheme.step: Metal: τ decreases, ρ rises (near-linear graph)

questions.stem_md: Explain the principle of a platinum resistance thermometer.

answer.model_answer_md: The resistance of a pure metal such as platinum **increases steadily** (nearly linearly) with temperature: $R_T = R_0(1 + \alpha\Delta T)$. By measuring the **resistance** of a platinum coil and knowing $R_0$ and α, the **temperature** can be calculated; platinum is stable and its α is reproducible.

questions.solution_md: R varies predictably with T.

**Reason (R):** The ions of warmer copper vibrate with a larger amplitude.

questions.stem_md: A 40 W lamp and a 100 W lamp, both rated 230 V, are wired in series across the 230 V mains. Which statement is correct?

options.text_md: The 40 W lamp dissipates 2.5 times as much power as the 100 W lamp
The 100 W lamp dissipates 2.5 times as much power as the 40 W lamp
The two lamps dissipate equal power
The 40 W lamp dissipates 1.6 times as much power as the 100 W lamp

questions.solution_md: R = V²/P, so R₄₀/R₁₀₀ = 100/40 = 2.5. In series the current is common and P = I²R ∝ R, so the 40 W lamp takes 2.5 times the power of the 100 W lamp — option (a).

questions.stem_md: A current of 2.0 A flows through a 10 Ω resistor for 5.0 minutes. Find the heat produced, in kJ.

A solar farm feeds 50 kW to a cold-storage unit along a cable pair of total resistance 0.50 Ω. Work out the heating loss in the cable when the power is delivered (a) at 250 V, (b) after a transformer raises it to 5000 V. What does the comparison show?

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) $I = \dfrac{50000}{250} = 200$ A; loss $= I^2R = 200^2 \times 0.50 = 20000$ W (20 kW).
(b) $I = \dfrac{50000}{5000} = 10$ A; loss $= 10^2 \times 0.50 = 50$ W.
Raising the voltage 20 times cuts the current 20 times and the $I^2R$ loss **400 times**: power is transmitted at high voltage.

questions.stem_md: (a) Distinguish the random (thermal) motion of free electrons in a metal from their drift, and say what the relaxation time is. [1] (b) Obtain the relation $I = n e A v_d$ for a conductor of cross-section A. [2] (c) A copper wire of cross-section 1.5 mm² carries 3.0 A (n = 8.5 × 10²⁸ m⁻³). Find the current density and the drift velocity, and explain why a lamp in the circuit lights almost instantly. [2]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) Random motion: fast (about $10^5$ m s$^{-1}$) in all directions, averaging to zero. Drift: the small average velocity (about $10^{-4}$ m s$^{-1}$) opposite to an applied field that gives the current. Relaxation time: the average time between successive collisions of a free electron with the ions.

(b) Electrons within a length $v_d\Delta t$ of a cross-section A cross it in time $\Delta t$: their number is $nAv_d\Delta t$ and charge $n e A v_d\Delta t$, so $I = n e A v_d$.

(c) $J = \dfrac{3.0}{1.5 \times 10^{-6}} = 2.0 \times 10^{6}$ A m$^{-2}$; $v_d = \dfrac{J}{n e} = \dfrac{2.0 \times 10^{6}}{8.5 \times 10^{28} \times 1.6 \times 10^{-19}} \approx 1.47 \times 10^{-4}$ m s$^{-1}$. The field that drives the electrons is established along the whole circuit almost instantly, so electrons everywhere, including in the filament, begin to drift at once.

questions.solution_md: Definitions; slice argument; numbers; field.

questions.stem_md: (a) A field E acts inside a metal that has n free electrons per unit volume with relaxation time τ. Obtain their drift speed, and hence show that the resistivity is ρ = m/(ne²τ). [3] (b) Silver has ρ = 1.6 × 10⁻⁸ Ω m and n = 5.9 × 10²⁸ m⁻³. Find the relaxation time. [1] (c) Using your expression, explain why the resistivity of silver rises when it is heated. [1]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) In field E, $a = eE/m$; averaged over collisions, $v_d = eE\tau/m$. $J = n e v_d = \dfrac{n e^2\tau}{m}E$; comparing with $J = \sigma E$, $\sigma = \dfrac{n e^2\tau}{m}$ and $\rho = \dfrac{m}{n e^2\tau}$.

(b) $\tau = \dfrac{m}{\rho n e^2} = \dfrac{9.1 \times 10^{-31}}{1.6 \times 10^{-8} \times 5.9 \times 10^{28} \times (1.6 \times 10^{-19})^2} \approx 3.77 \times 10^{-14}$ s.

(c) n is practically constant in a metal; heating increases ionic vibration, so collisions are more frequent and τ falls, making ρ larger.

questions.solution_md: Drift → J → σ → ρ; numbers; τ falls.

questions.stem_md: (a) Write the relation between resistance and resistivity, and state the factors on which resistivity depends. [1] (b) A constantan wire (ρ = 4.9 × 10⁻⁷ Ω m) is 3.0 m long and 0.50 mm in diameter. Find its resistance. [2] (c) The wire is stretched uniformly to twice its length. Find its new resistance. [1] (d) Suggest why standard resistors are wound from constantan and not from copper. [1]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) $R = \rho l/A$; ρ depends on the material and its temperature (not on the dimensions).

(b) $A = \pi(0.25 \times 10^{-3})^2 \approx 1.96 \times 10^{-7}$ m²; $R = \dfrac{4.9 \times 10^{-7} \times 3.0}{1.96 \times 10^{-7}} \approx 7.49$ Ω.

(c) Volume constant: length × 2, area ÷ 2, so $R' = 4R \approx 29.9$ Ω.

(d) Constantan has a very small temperature coefficient (and high resistivity), so its resistance hardly changes with temperature.

questions.solution_md: R = ρl/A; stretching; low α.

questions.stem_md: Overhead power lines are often made of aluminium rather than copper. Aluminium: ρ = 2.8 × 10⁻⁸ Ω m, density 2700 kg m⁻³. Copper: ρ = 1.7 × 10⁻⁸ Ω m, density 8900 kg m⁻³. (a) For cables of the same length and resistance, find the ratio of the cross-sectional area of the aluminium cable to that of the copper cable. [2] (b) Find the ratio of their masses. [2] (c) Use your results to explain the choice of aluminium. [1]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) Same $R$ and $l$: $\rho_\text{Al}/A_\text{Al} = \rho_\text{Cu}/A_\text{Cu}$, so $\dfrac{A_\text{Al}}{A_\text{Cu}} = \dfrac{2.8}{1.7} \approx 1.65$.

(b) Mass $= $ density × $Al$: $\dfrac{m_\text{Al}}{m_\text{Cu}} = \dfrac{2700 \times 2.8}{8900 \times 1.7} \approx 0.500$.

(c) Although the aluminium cable needs about 1.65 times the cross-section, it weighs only about half as much as an equally good copper cable, so the pylons can be lighter and further apart; aluminium is also cheaper.

questions.solution_md: A ∝ ρ; mass ∝ ρ × density.
